messages.subject: how could I possibly speedup my sampling with a simple reinforcement learning model?
parts:
Hey Stan,

we are recently considering migrating our simple reinforcement learning model from JAGS to Stan. 
However, when we tried the below Stan model, it wasn't really faster than running in JAGS with the same configuration (same samples/chain, burnin, thin, etc.) .
I was wondering if there is a way to speedup / optimize the code or sampling based on the current version?

PS: after reading previous posts, I've already used categorical_logit(), and I already cut the transformed data section to even simply the model, nonetheless it was still slow.
And it might be worth mentioning that, we have 130 subjects and 100 trials. 

Thanks in advance, any suggestion is appreciated!

cheers,
Lei


data {
  int<lower=1> nSubjects;                            // number of subjects
  int<lower=1> nTrials;                              // number of trials 
  int<lower=1,upper=2> choice[nSubjects,nTrials];    // 2nd choices, 1 or 2
  real<lower=-1,upper=1> reward[nSubjects,nTrials];  // outcome, 1 or -1
}

parameters {
  // group-level parameters
  real<lower=0,upper=1> lr_mu;
  real<lower=0,upper=1> lr_kappa0;
  real<lower=0,upper=1> temp0_mu;
  real<lower=0,upper=1> temp0_kappa0;

  // subject-level parameters
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[nSubjects] lr;
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[nSubjects] temp0;
}

transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> lr_kappa;
  real<lower=0> lr_a;
  real<lower=0> lr_b;
  real<lower=0> temp0_kappa;
  real<lower=0> temp0_a;
  real<lower=0> temp0_b;
  vector<lower=0,upper=20>[nSubjects] temp;

  lr_kappa <- 3.0 / (lr_kappa0 * lr_kappa0) - 1.0;
  lr_a <- lr_mu * lr_kappa;
  lr_b <- (1-lr_mu) * lr_kappa;

  temp0_kappa <- 3.0 / (temp0_kappa0 * temp0_kappa0) - 1.0;
  temp0_a <- temp0_mu * temp0_kappa;
  temp0_b <- (1-temp0_mu) * temp0_kappa;
  
  temp <- 20.0 * temp0;
}

model {

  row_vector[2] v[nTrials+1]; // values
  vector[nTrials] pe;         // prediction errors

  // hyperparameters, priors
  lr_mu ~ beta(1,1);
  lr_kappa0 ~ beta(1,1);
  temp0_mu ~ beta(1,1);
  temp0_kappa0 ~ beta(1,1);
  
  // subject loop and trial loop
  for (s in 1:nSubjects) {
    lr[s] ~ beta(lr_a,lr_b);
    temp0[s] ~ beta(temp0_a,temp0_b);

    v[1] <- rep_row_vector(0.0,2);

    for (t in 1:nTrials) {
      //* compute action probs using built-in softmax function and related to choice data */
      choice[s,t] ~ categorical_logit( temp[s] * v[t]' );

      //* prediction error */
      pe[t] <- reward[s,t] - v[t,choice[s,t]];

      //* value updating (learning) */
      v[t+1] <- v[t]; // make a copy of current value into t+1
      v[t,choice[s,t]] <- v[t,choice[s,t]] + lr[s] * pe[t]; // overwrite chosen value with pe update
    }
  }
}

Also, you want to use the same method of computing n_eff and Rhat.
The built-ins for R2jags are different and more liberal and from what
I see report effective sample sizes about twice as large as we report
in our more conservative approach in Stan (which uses cross-chain information
on the mean rather than only within chain information which imparts a positive
bias to the n_eff estimates).

I couldn't follow the parameterization --- why are all those variables
constrained to (0,1) and then manipulated with

parameters {
real<lower=0,upper=1> lr_kappa0;

transformed parameters {
lr_kappa <- 3.0 / (lr_kappa0 * lr_kappa0) - 1.0;

model {
lr_kappa0 ~ beta(1,1);

You don't need the beta(1,1) statements --- they're redundant in
Stan, but shouldn't be causing too much slowdown. Variables are by
default uniform on their declared constraints.

You probably want to define all the variables "temp..." as local
variables in the model block so they don't get saved and printed.
It takes both time and space to save them.

You should just declare v as a vector, then you don't have to
transpose.
> row_vector[2] v[nTrials+1]; // values
> vector<lower=0,upper=20>[nSubjects] temp;
> choice[s,t] ~ categorical_logit( temp[s] * v[t]' );

But if it's just size 2, don't you really want to be using a
bernoulli_logit instead of categorical_logit? The choices will
have to be 0:1 rather than 1:2, but otherwise should be the same.

- Bob

parts:
If the parameter estimates are different, then there is no use comparing run time. 

There are a few reasons that your parameter estimates are different. 
- the model was translated incorrectly; this is very common. It could be a mispecified distribution or a typo or a bug or...
- JAGS hasn't really converged; this is less common, but we see this when the posterior distribution is improper. 

I would start by double checking the translation. If you want exact replicability, then make sure the models are identical. Start with simulated data, make sure that fits equally in both. We did that when we started the project to evaluate whether Stan was working properly as an implementation of an MCMC algorithm. 

Then, move away from mathematical conveniences that were helpful in JAGS and start fitting the model you really want to fit. You're not limited by conjugate priors. There are HMC specific things that will make sampling faster.

But first things first. Fix the translation so the estimates are the same. 




Daniel

Hi Bob,

thanks for your comments and suggestions.

As you must have noticed, we were trying to fit a hierarchical model. 

First, taking the learning rate (lr) as an example. lr must be between 0 and 1, that's why we chose a beta distribution. lr_mu is the population mean of all the lr(s), lr_kappa is the concentration of the beta distribution. 
Our thought of using something like:

transformed parameters { 
        lr_kappa <- 3.0 / (lr_kappa0 * lr_kappa0) - 1.0;

is to prevent bimodal posterior beta distribution (such as beta(0.5,0.5) ). Or perhaps Stan is clever enough to prevent this case automatically?
Then, lr_mu and lr_kappa were used to derive lr_a and lr_b for the beta distribution at the individual level. 

Second, the idea for the temp parameter is basically the same, with temp could be a between 0 and 20. That's why we used the same procedure for temp0 and multiplied with 20 afterwards.
Based on your experience, would you suggest some other distribution for a positive parameter constrained at (0,n], instead of multiplying n with a beta?

Third, I've tried to declare v as a vector to avoid transpose, however there is an indexing error.

Steingrove, Wetzels & Wagenmakers (2013) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3847555/] used stan to fit a similar model, the PVL model which is kind of an extended RL model.
If I remember correctly, they did not use the beta distribution for the learning rate because they had convergence problems
(Though this was likely been with an earlier version of stan. I a writing this from memory, for details it would be best to contact the Helen Steingrove).

From my experience with fitting RL models a range of 20 for the temperature of the Luce/soft-max choice rule seems large.

An aside about avoiding bimodal learning rate distributions (on the group level): It is not unreasonable to assume a bimodal distribution, because if people learn by slowly accumulating payoff information, you get small learning rates (lets say < .2), but when people simply do win-stay lose-switch this behavior is best captured by high learning rates (close to 1). I have seen data where different participants used both these "strategies".

Guido

> That said, either a or b ought be larger than 1, but not both of them. How could I possibly constrain that? Or does it make much sense to you?

You can just replace the fmin with an fmax, then you're
guaranteed at least one is > 1. But...

Have you just tried constraining a > 0 and b > 0 and see
what the fit is? The problem is that constraints can often
lead to boundary behavior; if the fit with only the natural
constraints of a > 0 and b > 0 lead to a = 1/2 and b = 1/2, then

of min(a,b) > 1.

an unconstrained parameter (essentially an intercept only logistic
regression), then you won't get bimodal behavior.

model.
